commentary: Aquinas reads this chapter as a hinge: Book VII treated substance logically, through definition and its parts, while Book VIII turns to apply that groundwork to the natural substances actually before us. He recalls the earlier inventory - the substances everyone grants (the elements, plants and animals, the heavens) alongside the disputed ones some schools add (Forms, mathematical objects), and the further complication that genus and the universal were once mistaken for substance because Ideas ride on that same claim. Book VII, he notes, already dismantled the notion that genus or universal could be substance, and settled what a definition is and what its parts are. With that logical work behind him, Aristotle now resumes the sensible substances directly. Every one of them, Aquinas stresses, involves matter, and he distinguishes three ways "substance" gets used here: matter is substance only potentially, as that which is not yet a determinate thing but is capable of becoming one; form or actuality is substance as that which can be conceived, though not physically separated, apart from matter; and the composite of the two is substance in the fullest sense, since it alone is generated, destroyed, and capable of independent existence - form and matter themselves are never strictly generated, only the composite is. To prove matter's reality, Aquinas walks through the parallel with other kinds of change: motion in place, growth, and alteration all require some persisting subject beneath contrary states, and substantial change (coming-to-be and passing-away) requires the same kind of underlying subject, which is precisely what matter is. He cautions, though, that having matter for one kind of change does not entail having matter for every kind.

Having secured matter as substance-in-potency, Aquinas turns with Aristotle to substance as actuality, that is, form. He presents Democritus's view that all differences among things reduce to three material variations - shape, position, and arrangement - and then follows Aristotle in showing this is far too narrow: things also differ by manner of composition (mixing, binding, gluing, nailing), by position (lintel versus threshold), by time (breakfast versus dinner), by place (the different winds), and by sensible qualities like hardness or density. Aquinas's key move is to explain why this matters philosophically: each of these differentiae, though none of them is substance in the strict sense, plays the role of form relative to some matter, because it is precisely the differentia that completes a thing's definition and therefore accounts for its being. Just as within genuine substances actuality is what gets predicated of matter, so in every other case the differentia is what most resembles actuality. He walks through Aristotle's examples - a threshold is wood or stone lying in a certain position; a house is bricks and timber arranged in a certain way, possibly with a further purpose added; ice is water solidified in a certain manner; harmony is a certain blending of high and low tones. From this Aquinas draws a threefold classification of definitions: those who define by matter alone (stones and timber) describe only the potential thing; those who name only the arrangement or purpose describe the actuality; and those who state both, as Archytas characteristically did, capture the composite substance most completely, since the differentiating formula answers to form and the material formula to matter.

Aquinas treats this chapter as Aristotle's engagement with Plato's account of form, weighing four Platonist claims: that a species-name signifies form alone, not form-in-matter; that form is something beyond the material parts; that forms are ungenerated and incorruptible; and that forms exist apart from sensible things. On the first point, Aquinas notes that whether "house" names the composite or the shape alone matters little for the inquiry into sensible substance, since such substance is composite either way - but it matters for whether a thing is identical with its own essence. Where something is form alone, it simply is its quiddity, as soul is identical with what it is to be soul; where something is composite, thing and essence differ, since being a man is not the same as being this man. Turning to the second claim, Aquinas explains that a syllable is not merely its letters plus their juxtaposition, nor a house merely bricks plus arrangement, because the arrangement itself - the formal element - is not built from the material parts; rather the reverse holds, so man is not simply animal-plus-biped stacked together but something beyond the sum. He then answers the Antisthenean objection that a "what" cannot be defined, only likened to something else, as silver might be likened to tin: only composites can be defined, since a definitory formula predicates one element, as form, of another, as matter, while the ultimate simple constituents elude definition entirely. Finally he draws the analogy to number: a definition, like a number, divides into indivisible parts, changes species when anything is added or subtracted, and owes its unity not to being an aggregate or a bare point but to form actually determining matter.

Aquinas explains that Aristotle now examines material causation on its own terms. Though all generated things ultimately trace back to the same first matter and elements, each kind of thing nonetheless has a matter proper to itself - phlegm arises from what is sweet or fatty, bile from what is bitter - and several "matters" can be involved when one serves as matter for another further along the chain. The same matter can yield different products depending on the moving cause, as wood becomes either a chest or a bed, yet some products demand their own proper matter, since a saw cannot be fashioned from wool regardless of the agent at work; conversely, if one product genuinely can arise from different materials, the operative art or moving principle must be the same throughout. Aquinas stresses Aristotle's methodological point that a full causal account names all four causes, and that these must be proximate, not remote or generic - for man, not simply "fire and earth" but the specific matter, moving cause, formal cause (his essence), and final cause (his end, which Aquinas notes may coincide with the formal cause). He extends the inquiry to eternal natural substances, such as the heavens, which may have no matter at all, or only matter ordered to change of place rather than to generation and corruption; and to natural accidents, which strictly lack matter and instead have a substance as their subject. The eclipse illustrates this: the moon is the subject affected, the earth's interposition is the efficient cause, no final cause need be assigned since defects follow from natural necessity, and the definition becomes explanatory only once it incorporates that efficient cause. Sleep is treated similarly, requiring identification of the proper bodily subject and the precise affection involved.

Aquinas addresses the puzzle of things that begin or cease to be present without undergoing generation or corruption in the strict sense - points, and forms generally. It is not whiteness that comes to be, he explains, but the wood that comes to be white, since whatever properly comes to be does so from some underlying subject and becomes some determinate thing; bare forms, lacking such a subject of their own, are not properly generated but only said to arise incidentally. It follows that not everything has matter, but only what is capable of per se change into something else; what merely is or is not, without such transition, has no matter in the strict sense. Aquinas then works through the puzzle of how matter relates to contrary states: is a body's matter equally potential toward health and disease, is water equally potential toward wine and vinegar? His answer is that matter stands to the positive state, and to the form constituting it, directly and by its own nature, and to the privation or corruption of that state only secondarily, through the mediation of the form it first received. Thus water is properly the matter of wine, and becomes "matter" for vinegar only by way of wine's corruption; wine itself is not called potential vinegar, nor is a living man called potentially a corpse, because these are accidental corruptions - vinegar succeeds wine, and a corpse succeeds a living body, the way night succeeds day, rather than the way an effect arises from its matter. Aquinas concludes that anything undergoing this kind of transformation must first be resolved back into a more basic common matter before the new thing can emerge from it again.

Aquinas presents this chapter as Aristotle's resolution of an earlier puzzle: what makes a definition, or a number, genuinely one thing rather than a mere heap of parts - just as bodies achieve unity through contact or adhesion, a definition is one not by verbal stringing-together, as the Iliad is one poem only by convention, but by referring to a single reality. The sharpest form of the puzzle concerns man: why is he one thing rather than two, animal plus biped, especially on the Platonist supposition that Animal-itself and Biped-itself are separately subsisting Forms in which individual men merely participate - then a man would seem composed of two distinct participations rather than being truly single. Aquinas explains that so long as one treats the elements of a definition as detached universals needing to be glued together from outside, the puzzle cannot be solved. But once matter and form are recognized as related as potency to act, the difficulty dissolves, since asking what unites them is like asking what unites "round" and "bronze" in a bronze sphere: nothing further is needed beyond whatever causes the potential sphere to become actual, namely the efficient agent in things generated. Matter, he notes, can be sensible or purely intelligible, as in mathematics, where a circle is a plane figure, the surface functioning as matter and roundness as form; every definition contains an element of matter alongside one of actuality. But whatever has no matter at all is of itself, immediately, a unity, needing no further cause of its oneness, since being and unity are not separate genera standing over it. He closes by dismissing rival explanations, such as "participation" or calling the soul's union with the body a mere "communion," since these only restate the puzzle: proximate matter and form are, in truth, one and the same reality regarded first potentially, then actually.
